Hematopoiesis & Anemia I

How the blood is built — and the four ways the factory fails. Normal hematopoiesis, the stem cell hierarchy, the marrow niche, and impaired red cell production: iron, vitamin B12, folate, and inflammation.

How to use this file

The Blood Is a Liquid Organ

This block opens with a point worth holding onto: when you did gross anatomy, the blood was gone. Every other organ you could see and touch. This one drained away — and yet it carries oxygen, forms clots, and houses your immune system. These notes cover how that organ is built (hematopoiesis) and the first half of what goes wrong with its red cells (anemia from a production failure).

Abbreviations used in this sectionHSC hematopoietic stem cell — the self-renewing cell every blood cell descends from · RBC red blood cell, also called an erythrocyte · WBC white blood cell, also called a leukocyte · CBC complete blood count — the standard automated blood panel · Hgb hemoglobin — the oxygen-carrying protein, measured in grams per deciliter (g/dL) · Hct hematocrit — the percentage of whole blood volume that is red cells · MCV mean corpuscular volume — average red cell size, in femtoliters (fL) · MCH mean corpuscular hemoglobin — average hemoglobin content per red cell, in picograms (pg) · EPO erythropoietin — the kidney hormone that tells marrow to make red cells · TIBC total iron binding capacity — how much unfilled iron-carrying capacity transferrin has · AOCD anemia of chronic disease, also called anemia of inflammation
🔑 The three questions this file answers

1. Where does blood come from? One multipotent stem cell in the marrow, branching into myeloid and lymphoid lines. 2. How do we know someone is anemic? Hemoglobin or hematocrit below normal — then mean corpuscular volume tells you which bucket. 3. Which production failure is it? Iron, vitamin B12, folate, or inflammation. Those four cover most of what walks into a clinic.

🧠 The one framework the lecture returns to over and over

Every anemia lands in one of three buckets, and the lecture showed this slide repeatedly on purpose:

  • Blood loss — acute (trauma) or chronic (gastrointestinal tract, gynecologic).
  • Impaired red cell production — the factory is not making enough. This file.
  • Increased rate of destruction (hemolytic anemia) — the factory works, but the cells are being destroyed. Anemia Part 2.

Patients do not always fall neatly into one bucket — the lecture was explicit about that — but you need the buckets before you can notice when someone straddles two.

Hematopoiesis LO 1

Normal hematopoiesis · objective 1

What Hematopoiesis Is, and Where It Happens

Hematopoiesis is the process of blood cell production and development from hematopoietic stem cells. It begins in embryonic life and adapts throughout life inside specialized microenvironments.

Spin the tube: three layers, three stories

Draw whole blood and centrifuge it, and it separates into three layers. This one picture organizes the entire hematology block, because each layer belongs to a different set of diseases.

Spun whole blood — normal, anemic, and polycythemic. Hematocrit is literally the height of the red column.

LayerWhat is in itWhose disease is it
Plasma (top, straw-yellow)Water, coagulation proteins, albumin, immunoglobulins, hormones, nutrientsCoagulation and bleeding disorders
Buffy coat (thin middle band)White blood cells and plateletsWhite cell disorders and leukemias; platelet disorders
Erythrocytes (bottom, packed red)Red blood cells — the oxygen carriersThe anemias — this file and Part 2
⚠️ Plasma should be yellow

Hold onto the normal appearance. When you spin a tube and the plasma comes back pink or red instead of straw-yellow, that is free hemoglobin in the plasma — intravascular hemolysis. This recurs in Part 2 and again in the transfusion lecture as a bedside-visible emergency finding. Free heme is toxic to the kidneys.

Sites of hematopoiesis across a lifetime

  1. Embryo — the yolk sacThe first, primitive wave of blood formation happens outside the embryo proper, in the yolk sac.
  2. Fetus — liver and spleenThe fetal liver becomes the dominant site mid-gestation, with a contribution from the spleen.
  3. Late fetus onward — bone marrowMarrow takes over before birth and remains the site for the rest of life.
  4. Adult — the axial skeletonIn adults, hematopoiesis primarily occurs in the marrow of the vertebrae, ribs, sternum, and pelvis. The long bones convert to fatty (yellow) marrow.
🪝 Memory hook — “Yolk → liver → marrow, then the marrow retreats to the core”

Blood formation moves inward and upward over a lifetime: outside the embryo, then into the belly (liver and spleen), then into bone — and in adults it retreats out of the arms and legs into the axial skeleton. That last fact is why a marrow biopsy is taken from the pelvis and not the femur, and why the sternum and iliac crest are the sites you will hear named on the wards.

🩺 Why the site matters clinically

When marrow demand becomes extreme — severe chronic hemolysis, thalassemia major — the body can reactivate sites it abandoned. Extramedullary hematopoiesis in liver and spleen, and expansion of marrow cavities in the skull and face, produce the frontal bossing and maxillary prominence you will meet in the thalassemia case in Part 2.

Q: A centrifuged tube of a patient's blood shows a red column occupying 27% of the total height. Name the measurement, and estimate the hemoglobin.

Answer

The measurement is the hematocrit — 27%, which is the percentage of whole blood volume made up of red cells. Using the rule that hematocrit is roughly three times the hemoglobin, the hemoglobin is about 9 g/dL. The factor of three is a useful approximation, not a law.

Hematopoiesis LO 2

Normal hematopoiesis · objective 2

The Stem Cell Hierarchy and the Two Lineages

One cell type at the top, two great branches beneath it, and every blood cell you will ever name at the bottom. The hierarchy is the map — learn it once and the rest of hematology has somewhere to live.

Hematopoietic stem cells in red marrow give rise to red cells, white cells, and platelets.

🔑 What makes a stem cell a stem cell

Two properties, and you need both: self-renewal (it makes more copies of itself, so the supply never runs out) and differentiation (it makes committed daughter cells). Hematopoietic stem cells are multipotent — one cell can produce red cells, white cells, and platelets.

The contrast was drawn sharply in lecture: a stem cell that keeps dividing for your whole life is normal. Cancer is when a cell keeps dividing and is not supposed to. When hematopoietic stem cells make too many of themselves, that is leukemia.

The full hierarchy — hematopoietic stem cell to multipotent progenitors to the myeloid and lymphoid branches.

The myeloid branch

Erythrocyte

proerythroblast → mature red cell

Carries oxygen. Loses its nucleus on the way out of the marrow. A biconcave disc, extremely deformable, ~120-day lifespan.

Megakaryocyte

the giant of the marrow

A huge cell that stays in the marrow and blebs off fragments of its own membrane — those fragments, with no nucleus, are platelets.

Neutrophil

the first responder

The phrase used in lecture: the messy eaters. First to the site of infection, and the cause of a lot of the inflammation there. Multilobed nucleus.

Monocyte

circulates, then settles

Leaves the blood and becomes a macrophage (“like an amoeba, eating germs”) or a dendritic cell.

Eosinophil & basophil

the granular pair

Beautiful, brightly granulated cells, mostly involved in allergy and parasitic defense.

The lymphoid branch

T cell

educated in the thymus

Trained to tolerate self and destroy non-self — the single sentence that will also explain transfusion reactions and graft-versus-host disease.

B cell

matures in the bone marrow

Recognizes antigen, and on activation gives rise to plasma cells.

Plasma cell

the terminally differentiated B cell

The antibody factory — the humoral immune response.

NK cell

natural killer

Kills without prior sensitization; part of innate immunity.

🪝 Memory hook — “Myeloid does the work; lymphoid keeps the memory”

The myeloid line handles the physical jobs — carry the oxygen, plug the hole, eat the bacteria. The lymphoid line handles the intelligence job — remember what it has seen. That is exactly what a vaccine exploits: you show the lymphoid line a pathogen it does not have to survive, and it remembers.

Q: Which mature blood cell is not really a cell at all, and what does that fact explain about aspirin?

Answer

The platelet. It is a membrane fragment blebbed off a megakaryocyte and has no nucleus. Because it cannot transcribe new protein, an irreversible inhibitor such as aspirin disables it for its entire 7–10 day lifespan — the platelet cannot make replacement enzyme.

Q: A patient's bone marrow is packed with immature cells of a single myeloid line, crowding out everything else. What has gone wrong at the top of the hierarchy?

Answer

A hematopoietic stem or progenitor cell has begun self-renewing without differentiating — proliferation uncoupled from maturation. In the blood system that is leukemia. The marrow will look hypercellular, and the other lineages fail because they have been crowded out.

Hematopoiesis LO 3

Normal hematopoiesis · objective 3

Hormonal Regulation — Who Tells the Marrow What to Make

Each lineage has its own dispatcher. Learn the four hormones and you have also learned four drug classes, because in every case medicine has learned to give the hormone as a drug.

LineageProcess nameDevelopmental cellLab measurementHormonal regulationFunction
Red blood cellsErythropoiesisProerythroblast → mature erythrocyteHematocrit, hemoglobin, reticulocyte countErythropoietin — made by the kidneysCarry oxygen
PlateletsThrombopoiesisMegakaryocytes, via endomitosisPlatelet countThrombopoietinPrimary hemostasis
Neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, monocytesMyelopoiesisMyeloid progenitorsDifferential white blood cell countG-CSF and GM-CSF (colony-stimulating factors)Immune defense and inflammation
Lymphocytes (B, T, NK) and plasma cellsLymphopoiesisLymphoid progenitorsDifferential white blood cell countGrowth hormone, insulin-like growth factorIdentify and eliminate foreign antigens; immunologic memory
Abbreviations used in this sectionG-CSF granulocyte colony-stimulating factor — the drug form is filgrastim · GM-CSF granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor — the drug form is sargramostim · Endomitosis nuclear division without cell division — how a megakaryocyte becomes enormous and polyploid
🧠 Erythropoietin — the oxygen sensor loop

The kidney is continuously sampling how much oxygen is arriving. When tissue oxygen delivery falls — from anemia, from hypoxia, from altitude — the kidney releases erythropoietin, which drives division and differentiation of committed erythroid progenitors and pushes reticulocytes out into the blood.

The loop explains three separate clinical facts at once:

  • Chronic kidney disease causes anemia — the sensor and the factory foreman are the same organ, and it has failed.
  • Erythropoietin can be given as a drug (epoetin, darbepoetin) — you supply the missing order.
  • Inflammation blunts erythropoietin release — the mechanism behind anemia of chronic disease, later in this file.
🪝 Memory hook — “The kidney counts the oxygen, the marrow does the building”

If a question gives you an anemia with a low reticulocyte count and a creatinine that is climbing, the missing element is the order, not the raw material. Erythropoietin is the order. And the corollary repeated in the drug lectures: an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent is useless without iron — you can shout the order all you like, but the factory still needs bricks.

🩺 Reticulocyte count — the single most useful add-on test

A reticulocyte is a “baby red cell”, freshly released from the marrow and still carrying residual RNA. The count answers one question: is the marrow responding?

  • Low reticulocytes with anemia = a production problem. The factory is not responding. Everything in this file behaves this way.
  • High reticulocytes with anemia = the factory is working overtime, so the cells are being lost or destroyed. That is bleeding, or the hemolytic anemias of Part 2.

Q: A 68-year-old on dialysis has a hemoglobin of 8.4 g/dL, normal mean corpuscular volume, normal iron studies, and a low reticulocyte count. What is the mechanism, and what single laboratory value would you predict?

Answer

This is the anemia of chronic kidney disease. The failing kidney no longer makes enough erythropoietin, so the marrow is never told to build — hence the low reticulocyte count despite plenty of raw material. You would predict an inappropriately low erythropoietin level for that degree of anemia. Treatment is an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent, with iron stores repleted first.

Hematopoiesis LO 4

Normal hematopoiesis · objective 4

The Bone Marrow Niche

Stem cells do not float free. They live in a structured neighbourhood that decides whether they rest or divide — and that neighbourhood is itself a therapeutic target.

Normal bone marrow histology. The bright pink struts are bone trabeculae; the purple cellular slush between them is where blood is made.

🔑 Reading that picture

The bright pink struts are bone trabeculae — the internal scaffolding inside a bone that is hard on the outside. Between them sit the clear round holes (fat cells) and the dense purple cellular material — the maturing blood cells and, scattered among them, the stem cells themselves. The ratio of purple to white is cellularity, and it is the first thing a pathologist judges.

Components of the niche

1

Stromal cells

Fibroblasts, osteoblasts along the bone surface, adipocytes and endothelial cells. They physically anchor stem cells and secrete the signals that hold them in place.

2

Extracellular matrix

The structural mesh that provides adhesion sites. Losing adhesion is how a stem cell gets mobilized into the blood — the principle behind harvesting stem cells for transplant.

3

Blood vessels

The sinusoids, which supply nutrients and are the exit door. A reticulocyte squeezes through a sinusoidal wall to enter the circulation.

4

Signaling molecules

Cytokines and growth factors that set the balance between quiescence (rest) and activation (divide).

🧠 Quiescence is the point

The niche's real job is restraint. Most hematopoietic stem cells are quiescent most of the time. That is what protects the pool from exhaustion and from accumulating replication errors across a lifetime. The niche activates only as many stem cells as demand requires.

🩺 Why this is not abstract — three therapies live here
  • Stem cell transplantation. In its most basic form, you give a patient someone else's hematopoietic stem cells. But first you must empty the niche — high-dose chemotherapy ablates the marrow so the graft has somewhere to land.
  • Gene therapy. Take the patient's own stem cells, engineer them in the laboratory, and return them. Casgevy and Lyfgenia for sickle cell disease work exactly this way — and still require chemotherapy conditioning, which is why patients go through the same ordeal.
  • Cancer treatment. Chemotherapy that targets rapidly dividing cells hits the niche hardest of all. That is why marrow empties out, counts crash, and hair falls out.
🪝 Memory hook — The niche is a hotel, not a warehouse

A warehouse just stores things. A hotel has a front desk that decides who stays asleep in their room (quiescence), who gets called down to work (activation), and who checks out into the bloodstream. Disrupt the hotel and it does not matter how good your stem cells are — which is why every transplant begins by emptying the building.

Q: Why must a patient receive high-dose chemotherapy before an allogeneic stem cell transplant, and what does their marrow look like afterward?

Answer

Conditioning chemotherapy ablates the existing marrow — it clears the niche so the donor stem cells have physical space and signaling support to engraft, and it suppresses the recipient's immune system so the graft is not rejected. In malignancy it also serves to kill residual leukemic cells. Immediately afterward the marrow is hypocellular — The phrase used in lecture was that a biopsy at that point would look empty.

Hematopoiesis LO 5
Hematopoiesis LO 6

Normal hematopoiesis · objectives 5–6

Sampling the Marrow, and Reading Cellularity

Looking at the marrow is invasive, uncomfortable, and reserved for when you genuinely suspect marrow disease. Knowing when not to order it is as much of the objective as knowing how it is done.

Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy — prone position, posterior superior iliac spine.

  1. Position and siteThe patient lies prone. The operator palpates the posterior superior iliac spine — the same landmark you learned in osteopathic manipulative medicine — and preps and drapes it sterilely.
  2. AnesthesiaLocal anesthetic to skin and periosteum, plus at least mild sedation. Note that this takes real physical force, and it is usually performed by a hematologist-oncologist, not in the emergency department.
  3. AspirateA trocar is advanced through the cortex and marrow fluid is pulled into a syringe. This is squirted onto slides — it gives beautiful cytology: individual cell morphology, blast percentage, iron stain.
  4. Core biopsyA cylindrical core of bone is taken as well. This preserves architecture — the trabeculae, the fat-to-cell ratio, fibrosis, infiltration patterns — which an aspirate cannot show.
  5. ProcessingPathology prepares and stains the slides. The two specimens answer different questions and are almost always taken together.
🪝 Memory hook — Aspirate = the players; core = the stadium

The aspirate is a smear of loose cells — you see each player's face clearly but have no idea how they were arranged. The core keeps the seating plan: how full the stadium is, where the fibrosis is, whether an infiltrate is patchy or diffuse. Cellularity is a core-biopsy word, not an aspirate word.

Cellularity — the first read

Marrow cellularity — the ratio of hematopoietic cells to fat.

CellularityWhat you seeWhat it suggests
NormocellularA balanced mix of hematopoietic cells and fat, appropriate for the patient's ageNormal marrow
HypercellularPurple cells crowding out nearly all the fatLeukemia or another proliferative process — or a marrow driven hard by chronic hemolysis or blood loss (a compensatory hypercellularity)
HypocellularMostly fat, few hematopoietic cellsAplastic anemia, myelodysplastic syndrome, or the expected picture after chemotherapy or during stem cell transplant conditioning
⚠️ Do not order a marrow biopsy to work up a straightforward anemia

This was emphasized. Most anemia is diagnosed from blood drawn out of the arm — a complete blood count, red cell indices, iron studies, vitamin B12 and folate, a reticulocyte count, and a look at the smear. A marrow biopsy is reserved for suspected primary marrow disease: unexplained pancytopenia, suspected leukemia or myelodysplasia, staging a lymphoma, or confirming remission after treatment.

🩺 The exception worth knowing — the iron stain

You do not need a marrow biopsy to diagnose iron deficiency. But if one is done for another reason, a Prussian blue stain is the historical gold standard for marrow iron: blue granules present means stores exist, and their complete absence is diagnostic of iron deficiency. Both images appear in the iron section below.

Q: A 7-year-old finished induction chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukemia three weeks ago. A marrow biopsy shows a markedly hypocellular marrow with rare hematopoietic elements. Is this a treatment failure?

Answer

No — this is the expected and intended result. High-dose chemotherapy is given specifically to ablate the marrow and eliminate leukemic cells, so a hypocellular marrow at this point reflects the treatment working. The question that matters is whether residual leukemic blasts remain, and whether normal hematopoiesis subsequently recovers. Hypocellular is not a diagnosis on its own — it must be read against the clinical context.

Anemia I LO 1

Anemia part 1 · objective 1

Defining and Measuring Anemia

Two definitions, two measurements, and one thing worth understanding about each: what the instrument is actually doing when it hands you a number.

🔑 The two definitions — know both wordings
  • Physiologic definition — a reduction in the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood.
  • Laboratory definition — a reduction below normal limits of the total circulating red cell mass, as measured by hemoglobin concentration or hematocrit.

Hemoglobin and hematocrit are two genuinely different measurements of the same thing.

🧪

Hemoglobin (Hgb) — a direct chemical measurement

The instrument measures how much hemoglobin protein is present, usually by spectrophotometry — hemoglobin absorbs light at a characteristic wavelength.

  • Reported in grams per deciliter (g/dL).
  • Because hemoglobin is confined to red cells, it is an indirect measure of red cell mass.
  • Each hemoglobin molecule has four subunits — two alpha and two beta — and each subunit carries one molecule of oxygen, picked up in the lung and delivered to tissue.
  • The measurement favoured in the United Kingdom.
📏

Hematocrit (Hct) — a physical measurement

Spin whole blood and measure the height of the red column as a percentage of the total.

  • Reported as a percent. A hematocrit of 40% means 40% of that blood sample's volume is red cells.
  • Also called packed cell volume.
  • Normal ranges differ by sex: roughly 37–47% in females, 42–52% in males.
  • Elevated hematocrit is polycythemia, not anemia. The most common cause is an inherited trait.
  • The measurement favoured in the United States.
🪝 Memory hook — “Times three” — and why the ranges differ by sex

Hematocrit ≈ 3 × hemoglobin. A hemoglobin of 9 pairs with a hematocrit near 27; a hemoglobin of 12 pairs with a hematocrit near 36. It is an approximation, not a law, but it is how you sanity-check a value that looks wrong.

And when the class was asked why male and female reference ranges differ, the answer is simple: menstruation — a recurring monthly iron and blood loss across a large part of adult life. That same fact will drive the very first case in this file.

What anemia does to the patient

Whatever the underlying mechanism, reduced red cell mass and oxygen-carrying capacity produce a shared set of clinical features:

  • Pallor — pale skin, and best appreciated in conjunctivae, palmar creases, and nail beds.
  • Weakness and fatigue.
  • Dyspnea on exertion — the classic history is getting short of breath climbing stairs that used to be easy.
  • If severe enough: myocardial and central nervous system hypoxia. The brain does not tolerate significant anemia.
⚠️ Acute blood loss is a different clinical animal

The blunt version: all bleeding stops eventually — and if you bleed out, you die. With acute hemorrhage you lose whole blood: plasma volume and red cells together. Early on the hemoglobin can look deceptively normal, because the concentration has not changed yet — it falls once the intravascular volume is replaced. The immediate threat in acute bleeding is volume, not the number on the complete blood count.

Q: A 34-year-old is brought in after a motor vehicle collision with obvious hemorrhage. Her hemoglobin on arrival is 13.8 g/dL. Does this rule out significant blood loss?

Answer

No. In acute hemorrhage the patient loses plasma and red cells in the same proportion, so the concentration — which is what hemoglobin and hematocrit measure — is initially unchanged. The value falls only after fluid shifts into the intravascular space or resuscitation fluid is given, over hours. Manage the hemodynamics and the bleeding source, not the initial hemoglobin.

Anemia I LO 2

Anemia part 1 · objective 2

Classifying Anemia — Mechanism and Red Cell Indices

Two independent classification systems, and you use both at once. Mechanism tells you why; the red cell indices tell you which one.

System 1 — classification by mechanism

This is the slide the lecture returned to before every new topic, highlighting where it had reached. Learn the whole tree now; Part 2 lives entirely inside the middle branch.

BucketSubdivisionEntities
Blood lossAcuteTrauma
ChronicGastrointestinal tract; gynecologic disturbances
Increased rate of destruction
(hemolytic anemia)		Intrinsic — red cell membrane disordersHereditary spherocytosis
Intrinsic — red cell enzyme deficienciesGlucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency
Intrinsic — deficient globin chain synthesisThalassemias
Intrinsic — structurally abnormal globin chainsSickle cell disease
ExtrinsicAntibody-mediated destruction; mechanical trauma (microangiopathic hemolytic anemia); hypersplenism
Impaired red cell productionDefective hemoglobin synthesisIron deficiency
Defective DNA synthesisVitamin B12 and folate deficiency
Marrow response to inflammationAnemia of chronic disease
🪝 Memory hook — Factory, or the road home?

Reduce the tree to one question: is the problem in the factory, or on the road home?

  • Factory problem (impaired production) — not enough cells are being built. The reticulocyte count is low. This file.
  • Road-home problem (destruction or loss) — cells are built fine and then destroyed or lost, mostly peripheral to the marrow. The reticulocyte count is high because the factory is compensating. Part 2.

One cheap test — the reticulocyte count — splits the tree down the middle.

System 2 — classification by red cell indices

📐

Mean corpuscular volume (MCV) — how big is the cell?

  • < 80 fL — microcytic (too small)
  • 80–100 fL — normocytic (normal)
  • > 100 fL — macrocytic (too big)

This was called the critical discriminator, and that is right: the diagnoses parse according to this number. It is the second thing you look at, immediately after confirming the anemia itself.

🎨

Mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH) — how full is the cell?

Corpuscle is the old word for a red cell, so this is simply hemoglobin content per cell.

  • Normochromic — normal colour and normal central pallor
  • Hypochromic — pale, with an enlarged central pale zone: the cell could not be filled with enough hemoglobin
  • Hyperchromic — denser than normal, with loss of the central pallor
🧠 Why a red cell looks like a doughnut

A normal red cell is a biconcave disc — thick at the rim, thin in the middle. On a smear that thin middle reads as a pale circle: the central pallor, normally about one third of the cell's diameter. Put another way: it is a doughnut where they forgot to take the dough out of the middle.

The shape exists for a reason — it maximizes surface area for gas exchange and makes the cell extraordinarily deformable, so it can fold through capillaries narrower than itself. Two things go wrong with it, and each has its own section:

  • Not enough hemoglobin to fill it → the pale centre grows → hypochromia (iron deficiency, thalassemia).
  • The cytoskeleton fails and it balls up → the pale centre disappears → a spherocyte (Part 2). The image to hold: it stops being a doughnut and becomes a baseball.
🔑 The practical algorithm
  1. Confirm the anemiaHemoglobin or hematocrit below the sex-specific reference range.
  2. Look at the mean corpuscular volumeMicrocytic, normocytic, or macrocytic. This is where the differential splits.
  3. Get a reticulocyte countLow points to a production problem; high points to loss or destruction.
  4. Order the targeted studiesMicrocytic → iron studies. Macrocytic → vitamin B12 and folate. Normocytic with low reticulocytes → think inflammation, kidney disease, or early marrow disease.
  5. Look at the smearHypersegmented neutrophils, target cells, spherocytes, bite cells, and sickled cells are each nearly diagnostic on sight.
Mean corpuscular volumeThink first ofThen consider
Microcytic (< 80 fL)Iron deficiencyThalassemia; anemia of chronic disease (can be low-normal); sideroblastic anemia; lead poisoning
Normocytic (80–100 fL)Anemia of chronic disease; acute blood lossChronic kidney disease; early iron deficiency; hemolysis; marrow failure
Macrocytic (> 100 fL)Vitamin B12 or folate deficiencyAlcohol; liver disease; hypothyroidism; myelodysplastic syndrome; drugs (methotrexate, hydroxyurea, zidovudine); marked reticulocytosis

Q: A patient has a hemoglobin of 10.1 g/dL with a mean corpuscular volume of 89 fL. A colleague says the normal MCV rules out a nutritional deficiency. Where is the flaw?

Answer

A normal mean corpuscular volume is an average. A patient with both iron deficiency (microcytic) and vitamin B12 or folate deficiency (macrocytic) can average out to a perfectly normocytic value — a real and common situation in malnutrition, malabsorption, and the elderly. Two clues expose it: a raised red cell distribution width, and a smear showing a dimorphic population of both small pale cells and large oval ones. The same point comes up in the cases — patients do not always have exactly one diagnosis.

Anemia I LO 3

Anemia part 1 · objective 3 · impaired production

Iron Metabolism and Iron Deficiency Anemia

The most common nutritional deficiency in the world. A warning from lecture: iron seems like it should be simple, and it is genuinely not — because there are four separate places along the pathway where it can go wrong, and the laboratory pattern tells you which.

Abbreviations used in this sectionFe²⁺ ferrous iron — the reduced, absorbable form · Fe³⁺ ferric iron — the oxidized form; must be reduced before it can be absorbed · TIBC total iron binding capacity — a measure of how many empty iron-binding sites transferrin has · Transferrin the plasma protein that carries iron through the blood · Ferritin the intracellular protein that stores iron; the serum level reflects total body stores · FOBT fecal occult blood test — checks stool for blood not visible to the eye

Where the iron is

CompartmentShare of total body ironDetail
Functional iron80%Hemoglobin, myoglobin, and iron-containing enzymes
Storage iron20%Ferritin and hemosiderin, chiefly in liver and macrophages
Total body iron — women2–3 gLower stores, ongoing menstrual losses
Total body iron — men4–6 gLarger reserve

The iron cycle — absorption, transport, utilization, storage. Each panel is a place the pathway can break.

🔑 Four stations — and four ways to fail
  1. Duodenum — absorptionDietary iron is absorbed in the duodenum, and only as Fe²⁺. Roughly 1–2 mg per day is absorbed. Fails in: celiac disease, chronic diarrhea, gastrectomy or bypass, and acid suppression.
  2. Plasma — transport on transferrinTransferrin carries about 3 mg of Fe³⁺ at any moment. Picture it as a molecule with little cups that may be full or empty — this image is the whole basis of the TIBC. Fails in: rare transferrin disorders.
  3. Cells — utilizationIron is delivered to the marrow for erythropoiesis (~2500 mg sits in circulating erythrocytes) and to muscle for myoglobin (~500 mg). Fails in: anemia of chronic disease, where iron exists but cannot be released to the erythroid precursors.
  4. Liver and macrophages — storageRoughly 1000 mg is stored as ferritin and hemosiderin. Senescent red cells are recycled here. Fails in: depletion from chronic loss — the first pool to empty.
🪝 Memory hook — Ferritin is the fuel gauge; transferrin saturation is the fuel line

Ferritin tells you what is in the tank — it is the earliest thing to fall, before the hemoglobin ever moves. Transferrin saturation tells you what is reaching the engine right now. You can have a full tank and a blocked line — that is anemia of chronic disease, two sections down.

How people become iron deficient

1

Dietary lack

Rare in industrialized countries with abundant food, but real in the elderly, infants and children on restricted diets, and infants fed largely on breast milk or cow's milk, which contain very little bioavailable iron. the lecture sees this in the emergency department in toddlers who “only want milk.”

2

Impaired absorption

Sprue (celiac disease), chronic diarrhea, gastrectomy and bariatric surgery — anything that removes or bypasses the duodenum, or removes gastric acid.

3

Increased requirements

Growing infants and children, and pregnancy.

4

Chronic blood loss

The most important cause in the Western world. Gastrointestinal: ulcers, hemorrhoids, cancer. Female genital tract: menorrhagia, uterine cancer.

⚠️ The single highest-yield sentence in this lecture

Iron deficiency in an adult male or a postmenopausal woman should be considered to be caused by gastrointestinal blood loss until proven otherwise.

The reason is stated plainly on the slide and in the lecture: gastrointestinal cancer — adenocarcinoma of the colon in particular — can present with iron deficiency anemia and nothing else. The patient is bleeding into the stool, does not know it, and the loss is chronic and insidious. That is why iron deficiency in this group triggers a fecal occult blood test and endoscopic evaluation, not just a prescription for iron.

Iron deficiency is a symptom, not a final diagnosis. Always ask where the iron went.

Morphology

Iron deficiency produces a hypochromic microcytic anemia: the cells are paler (not enough hemoglobin to fill them) and smaller than normal.

Iron deficiency smear — note how much of each cell is central pallor. Microcytosis is harder to judge by eye without a normal cell for comparison.

The mechanism in one line — four irons are needed for four globin subunits.

🧠 Why iron deficiency makes cells small as well as pale

An erythroid precursor divides while it accumulates hemoglobin, and it stops dividing once it reaches a target hemoglobin concentration. Without iron it cannot reach that concentration on schedule, so it undergoes an extra division or two before maturing. Each division halves the cell. The result is both microcytic and hypochromic — one mechanism, two findings.

Contrast this with vitamin B12 and folate deficiency, where the cytoplasm matures normally but the nucleus cannot divide — so the cell ends up too big. Same organ, opposite direction, and the reason mean corpuscular volume splits the differential so cleanly.

Marrow iron — the Prussian blue stain

Normal marrow — stainable blue iron granules are present.

Iron deficiency — the diagnostic finding is the absence of blue.

🩺 You almost never need this — but you must be able to read it

You do not order a marrow biopsy to diagnose iron deficiency. But when a marrow is obtained for another reason, the Prussian blue stain is the historical gold standard, and the finding in iron deficiency is decreased to absent stainable iron. It is also how you catch iron deficiency hiding underneath another marrow disorder.

Laboratory diagnosis

TestLevel in iron deficiencyWhy
Serum iron (Fe)DecreasedLess iron in circulation
Ferritin (stored iron)DecreasedStores are the first pool to empty — the earliest and most useful marker
Total iron binding capacityIncreasedTIBC reflects the transferrin binding sites not saturated with iron. Low serum iron leaves more empty cups, so the capacity to bind goes up
Transferrin saturationDecreased (< 15%)The same fact stated the other way round — the cups are empty
Mean corpuscular volumeDecreased (< 80 fL; normal 80–100)Extra divisions before maturation
Bone marrow ironDecreased to absentNo stainable Prussian blue
🪝 Memory hook — Empty cups, high capacity

The TIBC is the one students reliably get backwards, and lecture flagged it as the tricky one. Hold the picture: transferrin is a molecule carrying cups. When you are iron deficient the cups are floating around empty — so the capacity to bind more iron is high. Empty cups = high TIBC = low saturation.

Now flip it for the section below: in anemia of chronic disease the body deliberately hides iron, and it also makes less transferrin. Fewer cups on the shelf = low TIBC. That single difference separates the two most commonly confused anemias in the hospital.

⚠️ Ferritin is an acute phase reactant

This is the caveat that makes iron studies harder than they look. Ferritin rises in inflammation, infection, liver disease, and malignancy regardless of iron stores. So a genuinely iron-deficient patient who is also acutely sick can have a normal or even elevated ferritin.

The consequence, as put in lecture: diagnosing anemia is never one test. Interpret ferritin alongside transferrin saturation, TIBC, C-reactive protein, and the smear.

🩺 Treatment — and why it fails
  • Oral iron supplementation plus dietary change is first line, together with correcting the underlying cause.
  • Adherence is the real obstacle. The lecture was blunt: oral iron has a ton of gastrointestinal side effects — nausea, constipation, metallic taste, black stools — and patients quit.
  • Diet alone will not correct an established deficiency. Once someone is genuinely deficient you have to replete stores, not just improve intake.
  • Expect a reticulocyte rise within about a week if the treatment is working.

Q: A 58-year-old man has a hemoglobin of 10.8 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume 73 fL, ferritin 8 ng/mL, and transferrin saturation 9%. He has no symptoms other than fatigue. What is the diagnosis, and what is the next step?

Answer

The diagnosis is iron deficiency anemia — microcytic, with low ferritin and low transferrin saturation. The next step is not to prescribe iron and stop there. In an adult male, iron deficiency is presumed to be gastrointestinal blood loss until proven otherwise, so he needs evaluation for a gastrointestinal source — fecal occult blood testing and, importantly, endoscopic evaluation to exclude colorectal carcinoma. Treat the iron and find the leak.

Q: Explain why the total iron binding capacity is HIGH in iron deficiency but LOW in anemia of chronic disease.

Answer

TIBC measures unsaturated transferrin binding sites. In iron deficiency there is little iron to occupy those sites and the liver increases transferrin production, so unbound capacity is high. In anemia of chronic disease, inflammation both reduces transferrin synthesis (it is a negative acute phase reactant) and sequesters iron inside macrophages, so there are fewer binding sites overall and the TIBC is low to normal even though serum iron is also low.

Four iron studies, one diagnosis. This is the discrimination the exam tests and the one that changes management — give iron to an inflamed patient and it goes nowhere.

Defective DNA Synthesis — Vitamin B12, Pernicious Anemia, and Folate

Iron deficiency breaks hemoglobin synthesis and gives you small cells. Vitamin B12 and folate deficiency break DNA synthesis and give you big ones. Same organ, opposite direction — and one of the two also destroys the spinal cord.

Abbreviations used in this sectionB12 vitamin B12, also called cobalamin · IF intrinsic factor — the protein from gastric parietal cells that B12 must bind to be absorbed · MMA methylmalonic acid — a metabolite that accumulates when B12 is deficient · THF tetrahydrofolate — the active form of folate · PA pernicious anemia — autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor · SCD (here) subacute combined degeneration — degeneration of the dorsal and lateral spinal columns

Two vitamins, one pathway

The shared pathway. Folate feeds DNA synthesis; B12 sits at the homocysteine-to-methionine step — which is why they present identically.

🔑 Vitamin B12 has two jobs, and that is the whole clinical picture
  • DNA synthesis — shared with folate. Failure here produces the megaloblastic anemia.
  • Maintenance of the myelin surrounding neurons — B12 only. Failure here produces the neurologic complications, which eventually become irreversible.

Folate has only the first job. That single asymmetry is the most testable fact in this section.

Megaloblastic morphology

Megaloblastic smear — oval macrocytes and a hypersegmented neutrophil.

  • Erythrocytes are larger than normal (macrocytic) and oval shaped — the term is macro-ovalocytes.
  • Neutrophils are larger and hypersegmented, with five to six or more nuclear lobules. A normal neutrophil has three to five.
  • The bone marrow is hypercellular, with large red cell precursors containing fine, open chromatin — the megaloblasts — plus enlarged granulocyte precursors (giant bands and metamyelocytes).
  • All of these changes result from inadequate DNA synthesis, with impaired nuclear maturation and cell division.
🧠 Nuclear–cytoplasmic asynchrony — the one idea behind every finding

Hemoglobin synthesis in the cytoplasm proceeds normally, because it needs iron, not DNA. Nuclear maturation and cell division stall, because they need thymidine, which needs folate, which needs B12 to be regenerated. The cytoplasm outruns the nucleus.

Every finding drops out of that one sentence:

  • The cell keeps growing but cannot divide → it ends up too big (macrocytic).
  • The nucleus stays immature → fine, open chromatin in the marrow precursors.
  • The defect is not red-cell-specific — it hits every dividing cell → hypersegmented neutrophils and giant bands.
  • Many precursors die in the marrow before release → ineffective erythropoiesis, which is why the marrow is hypercellular while the reticulocyte count is low and the lactate dehydrogenase is elevated.
🪝 Memory hook — The hypersegmented neutrophil is the giveaway

A macrocytosis has a long differential — alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, drugs, reticulocytosis. But a hypersegmented neutrophil on the smear says the problem is specifically DNA synthesis, which narrows you immediately to B12 or folate. the class was asked the class to remember normal neutrophil lobes for exactly this reason. Count the lobes: six or more, think megaloblastic.

Vitamin B12 metabolism — a long road with many exits

B12 absorption — every arrow on this diagram is a place a deficiency can start.

  1. DietThe major source is animal products. Plants and vegetables contain very little cobalamin — which is why strict vegans are at genuine risk.
  2. Stomach — liberationGastric pepsin and acid liberate B12 from its dietary binding proteins. Salivary haptocorrin then binds it and carries it onward.
  3. Stomach — intrinsic factorParietal cells of the gastric mucosa secrete intrinsic factor. These are the same cells that make gastric acid — remember that pairing.
  4. Duodenum — the handoffPancreatic proteases split the haptocorrin–B12 complex, freeing B12 to bind intrinsic factor and form the B12–intrinsic factor complex.
  5. Terminal ileum — absorptionThe complex is absorbed via the cubilin receptor in the terminal ileum. This is the only place it happens.
  6. Blood — transportB12 binds transcobalamin II, which delivers it to the cells of the body.
Cause of B12 deficiencyExamples
Inadequate dietStrict vegan diet, severe malnutrition
Impaired absorption — intrinsic factor deficiencyPernicious anemia; gastrectomy and bariatric surgery
Impaired absorption — malabsorption statesSprue (celiac disease), ileal resection, Crohn disease and other ileal inflammation
Competitive uptakeParasitic infection (fish tapeworm, Diphyllobothrium latum); intestinal bacterial overgrowth
Increased requirementPregnancy
🩺 Bariatric surgery is a modern, common cause

This was called out specifically. Sleeve gastrectomy and gastric bypass remove or bypass the acid- and intrinsic-factor-producing stomach, and bypass the duodenum. The result is a predictable long-term deficiency of B12 and iron together. These patients need lifelong monitoring and supplementation, and it is a common source of the mixed micro-plus-macrocytic picture that averages out to a normal mean corpuscular volume.

Pernicious anemia

Pernicious anemia — the autoimmune chain of events.

🔑 Pernicious anemia is an autoimmune disease, not a diet problem

The name sounds generic but means something quite specific: autoimmune destruction of the gastric mucosa leading to loss of parietal cells, which produce intrinsic factor. Without intrinsic factor there is no B12–IF complex, and therefore no absorption in the terminal ileum — no matter how much B12 the patient eats.

AntibodyFrequency in pernicious anemia
Anti-parietal cell antibody85–90% of patients — more sensitive
Anti-intrinsic factor antibody75% of patients — more specific

Tissue changes in pernicious anemia — three organs, not one

1

Megaloblastic anemia

Macro-ovalocytes, hypersegmented neutrophils, hypercellular marrow — from B12 deficiency.

2

Gastric atrophy with intestinal metaplasia

From the immune-mediated destruction itself. Consequence: a greater risk of developing gastric carcinoma — these patients need ongoing surveillance.

3

Central nervous system lesions

Myelin degeneration of the dorsal and lateral columns of the spinal cord — the severe form is called subacute combined degeneration. From B12 deficiency.

⚠️ Treating pernicious anemia means treating three problems

This point was made directly: you are not just giving more B12. You are managing an autoimmune gastritis with cancer risk, a hematologic deficiency, and a neurologic degeneration. And B12 must be given by a route that does not require intrinsic factor — intramuscular injection, or high-dose oral therapy relying on passive diffusion.

The Schilling test — historical, but it teaches the anatomy

🩺 How it worked, and why it is worth understanding

No longer performed, but it localizes the lesion better than any single modern test, which is why it is still taught. The framing from lecture: these pathways are confusing, and there is no single test that just says “here is the diagnosis.”

  1. Saturate the bodyThe patient is given an injection of non-radioactive B12 to saturate all tissue binding sites, so any absorbed oral dose must spill into the urine.
  2. Stage I — oral radiolabeled B12 aloneA radiolabeled oral dose is given and a 24-hour urine collected. Radiolabel absent from the urine = the oral dose was not absorbed.
  3. Stage II — repeat WITH intrinsic factorRepeat, this time giving exogenous intrinsic factor alongside. If the radiolabel now appears in the urine, the missing ingredient was intrinsic factor — pernicious anemia.
  4. Still absent?If B12 is still not detected despite exogenous intrinsic factor, the defect is absorption at the terminal ileum — ileitis, ileal resection, or bacterial overgrowth.

Folate deficiency

🔑 Identical anemia, no neurology

Folate deficiency produces a megaloblastic anemia identical to that of B12 deficiency. The difference: the neurologic manifestations of B12 deficiency do not occur.

Folate is also the key nutrient in pregnancy for neural tube closure — which is why every prenatal vitamin contains it, and why supplementation prevents spina bifida.

Cause of folate deficiencyExamples
Decreased intakeInadequate diets of chronic alcoholics and people who are indigent or food-insecure. Richest dietary source is green vegetables.
Increased requirementPregnancy and infancy
Impaired utilizationFolate antagonists — chemotherapeutic agents, notably methotrexate
🧠 Why chemotherapy targets folate

The reasoning from lecture, worth reproducing because it explains chemotherapy toxicity generally: chemotherapy is, broadly, a poison aimed at fast-dividing cells. What are fast-dividing cells busy doing? DNA synthesis. So shut down DNA synthesis — and the folate pathway is the obvious lever.

That is also why the side effects are predictable: the fastest-dividing normal tissues suffer first. The marrow empties out, the gut mucosa ulcerates, and the hair falls out.

Telling B12 and folate apart

Test or findingB12 deficiencyFolate deficiency
Mean corpuscular volumeIncreased (>100 fL)Increased (>100 fL)
Blood smearHypersegmented neutrophils, macro-ovalocytesHypersegmented neutrophils, macro-ovalocytes
Neurologic examinationAbnormal — paresthesias, sensory ataxia; severe: subacute combined degenerationNormal — no neurologic manifestations
Methylmalonic acidElevatedNormal
HomocysteineElevatedElevated
Serum B12LowNormal
Serum and red cell folateNormalLow
AutoantibodiesPresent if pernicious anemia (anti-parietal cell, anti-intrinsic factor)Absent
Response to folateHematologic improvement, but neurologic damage progressesPrompt hematologic improvement
🪝 Memory hook — “MMA rises with B12 — the M's go together”

Methylmalonic acid is elevated in B12 deficiency and normal in folate deficiency. Homocysteine goes up in both, so it cannot discriminate — it only tells you one of the two is missing. If you can only order one test to separate them, order the methylmalonic acid.

And the clinical mnemonic for the sequence: B12 has the Brain. Folate does not.

⚠️ Never give folate alone to a macrocytic anemia

Directly from the slide footnote: the anemia caused by B12 deficiency may improve with the administration of folate; however, folate has no effect on the neurologic manifestations of B12 deficiency.

The trap is real. You correct the blood count, everyone relaxes, the patient looks better — and the subacute combined degeneration keeps progressing toward irreversibility. Always check a B12 level before treating a megaloblastic anemia with folate.

Q: A 62-year-old woman has a hemoglobin of 9.4 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume 112 fL, hypersegmented neutrophils, elevated homocysteine, and a normal methylmalonic acid. What is the deficiency, and what must you check before treating?

Answer

Folate deficiency. The homocysteine is raised in both deficiencies, but the normal methylmalonic acid excludes B12. Before starting folic acid you must still check a B12 level, because a coexisting B12 deficiency would be masked hematologically by folate replacement while the neurologic degeneration continued unopposed.

Q: Why is the reticulocyte count LOW in megaloblastic anemia even though the bone marrow is HYPERCELLULAR?

Answer

Because of ineffective erythropoiesis. Precursors are produced in large numbers — hence the hypercellular marrow — but they cannot complete nuclear division and are destroyed within the marrow before ever being released. Few mature cells reach the blood, so the reticulocyte count is low, and the intramedullary cell death releases lactate dehydrogenase and indirect bilirubin, which is why the LDH is elevated.

Anemia of Chronic Disease

The most common cause of anemia among hospitalized patients in the United States — and the one that most often gets mistaken for iron deficiency and treated with iron that does nothing.

🔑 What it is
  • Impaired red cell production associated with chronic disease. Also called anemia of inflammation.
  • The most common cause of anemia among hospitalized patients in the United States.
  • It is associated with defective iron utilization, and therefore may mimic iron deficiency.
CategoryClassic examples
Chronic infectionsOsteomyelitis, lung abscess, endocarditis
Chronic immune disordersRheumatoid arthritis, Crohn disease
NeoplasmsHodgkin disease, carcinoma
🧠 What every entry on that list has in common

The question was put to the class and answered it in one word: inflammation. Not the infection, not the tumour, not the joint — the cytokine response to all three. That is why a single mechanism covers such a scattered list of diseases.

The mechanism — one inflammatory stimulus, four separate hits on erythropoiesis.

Four mechanisms, one stimulus

A

Hepcidin goes up

Interleukin-6 drives hepatic synthesis of hepcidin. Hepcidin inhibits iron release from macrophages and enterocytes, so recycled and dietary iron is trapped where it sits. Serum iron falls even though total body iron is normal or high.

B

Erythropoietin release is inhibited

Cytokines blunt erythropoietin release from the kidney, so the erythropoietic drive is reduced — the order is never given loudly enough.

C

Erythroid proliferation is inhibited

The cytokines act directly on erythroid precursors to suppress their proliferation, independent of iron and erythropoietin.

D

Hemophagocytosis is augmented

Activated macrophages of the reticuloendothelial system begin consuming red cells. As put in lecture: they should not be doing that — but the hospital is full of patients whose macrophages are, and they are the sickest patients there.

🪝 Memory hook — Hepcidin is the doorman who locks the exits

Ferroportin is the only door iron has out of a gut cell or a macrophage. Hepcidin destroys ferroportin. High hepcidin means the doors are locked — the iron is in the building, it just cannot get to the marrow.

That one image explains the whole laboratory picture and the treatment failure: ferritin high (iron is stored and ferritin is also an acute phase reactant), serum iron low (none is circulating), and oral iron does not work — you are shoving more iron at a locked door.

Laboratory diagnosis

TestLevel or finding in anemia of chronic disease
Mean corpuscular volumeLow to normal (normal 80–100 fL) — usually normocytic, sometimes mildly microcytic
Blood smearRed cells are normochromic or hypochromic
Serum ironLow
Total iron binding capacityDecreased to normal
FerritinElevated
Bone marrowIncreased iron in macrophages — the iron is present, but sequestered rather than trafficked out
Reticulocyte countLow — a production problem
🩺 Treatment

The anemia of chronic disease is generally mild, and treatment of the underlying condition corrects the anemia. That is the whole management strategy, and it is worth saying plainly because the instinct to “treat the number” is strong.

  • Treat the underlying disease. Control the rheumatoid arthritis, drain the abscess, treat the cancer.
  • Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents may be considered if the patient is symptomatic — but there are real safety concerns, and severity should guide the decision.
  • Optimize the diet, especially in older patients who may have concurrent nutritional deficiencies and may be eating poorly or living alone.
  • Oral iron generally does not help, because the problem is not iron supply — it is iron release.

The discrimination that matters most

TestIron deficiency anemiaAnemia of chronic diseaseBoth together
Mean corpuscular volumeLow (<80)Low to normalLow
Serum ironLowLowLow
FerritinLowNormal to highLow-normal (may be misleading)
Total iron binding capacityHighLow to normalVariable
Transferrin saturationLow (<15%)LowLow
Marrow ironAbsentIncreased, in macrophagesReduced
Reticulocyte countLowLowLow
⚠️ The two tests that actually separate them

Serum iron is low in both, so it discriminates nothing. The pair that does the work is ferritin and total iron binding capacity, and they move in opposite directions:

  • Iron deficiency: ferritin LOW, TIBC HIGH. Empty tank, extra empty cups.
  • Anemia of chronic disease: ferritin HIGH, TIBC LOW. Full tank, locked doors, fewer cups.

And remember the confounder that makes this hard in real patients: ferritin is an acute phase reactant, so a genuinely iron-deficient patient who is also inflamed can show a normal ferritin. When the picture is mixed, the transferrin saturation and a marrow iron stain settle it.

Q: A 71-year-old with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis has a hemoglobin of 9.6 g/dL, MCV 86 fL, serum iron low, ferritin 340 ng/mL, TIBC low, and a low reticulocyte count. Would oral iron help? Why or why not?

Answer

No. This is anemia of chronic disease. Inflammatory cytokines — chiefly interleukin-6 — raise hepcidin, which degrades ferroportin and blocks iron export from macrophages and enterocytes. Total body iron is adequate (high ferritin, low TIBC, increased marrow macrophage iron); it simply cannot be released to erythroid precursors. Adding oral iron does not open that door. The treatment is control of the underlying rheumatoid arthritis, with an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent considered only if she is symptomatic.

Case Review — Building the Diagnostic Approach

Four cases from lecture, all inside the impaired red cell production circle. Read the presentation, commit to an answer, then reveal. Note how in each one a single laboratory value does the discriminating work.

🔑 The approach these cases are drilling
  1. Confirm anemiaHemoglobin below the reference range for sex.
  2. Read the mean corpuscular volume FIRSTMicrocytic, normocytic, or macrocytic. As put in lecture: you look at the MCV first and you go — are the cells big or small?
  3. Add the reticulocyte countLow confirms you are still inside the production bucket.
  4. Order the discriminating studyFerritin for microcytic. B12, folate, and methylmalonic acid for macrocytic. Inflammatory markers and full iron studies for normocytic.
  5. Read the smearHypersegmented neutrophils change the answer on their own.

Case 1 — 25-year-old woman

🧍

Presentation

  • Fatigue, shortness of breath, pale skin
  • Pica — craving and chewing ice
  • History of heavy menstrual bleeding
  • Vegetarian diet
🧪

Laboratory

  • Hemoglobin 7 g/dL
  • Mean corpuscular volume 74 fL — microcytic
  • Ferritin low

Q: Before you read on — what is your diagnosis, and what is the single lab value that settles it?

Answer

Iron deficiency anemia, due to menstrual blood loss plus dietary insufficiency. Microcytic anemia with a low ferritin is iron deficiency until proven otherwise, and the ferritin is the value that settles it. Pica — the craving for non-nutritive substances, classically ice (pagophagia) — is a distinctive and highly suggestive clue. She has both mechanisms at once: chronic loss through menorrhagia and reduced intake of bioavailable iron. Note that in a premenopausal woman with obvious menorrhagia, you do not automatically pursue a gastrointestinal source — that rule applies to adult males and postmenopausal women.

Management: Oral iron supplements and dietary change. Warn her about the gastrointestinal side effects up front — nausea, constipation, and black stools are the reason most patients stop. Continue iron after the hemoglobin normalizes to refill stores.

Case 2 — 61-year-old man

🧍

Presentation

  • Fatigue, mild confusion, pallor
  • Paresthesias
  • No fever, no bleeding
  • Prior gastric issues suspected
🧪

Laboratory

  • Hemoglobin 6.3 g/dL
  • Mean corpuscular volume 115 fL — macrocytic
  • Vitamin B12 140 pg/mL — low
  • Lactate dehydrogenase elevated
  • Reticulocyte count low
  • Smear: hypersegmented neutrophils, macrocytosis

Q: Before you read on — what is your diagnosis, and what is the single lab value that settles it?

Answer

Megaloblastic anemia due to vitamin B12 deficiency, most likely from pernicious anemia. Macrocytic anemia with hypersegmented neutrophils means defective DNA synthesis; the low B12 names which one. The paresthesias and confusion are the tell that this is B12 and not folate — folate deficiency has no neurologic manifestations. Two supporting findings are worth reading properly: the elevated LDH with a low reticulocyte count is the signature of ineffective erythropoiesis, where precursors are made and then destroyed inside the marrow. The prior gastric history points at loss of intrinsic factor.

Management: Intramuscular vitamin B12 injections, which bypass the need for intrinsic factor, with rapid clinical improvement. Confirm the cause with anti-parietal cell and anti-intrinsic factor antibodies, and remember the associated gastric carcinoma risk requires ongoing surveillance.

Case 3 — 50-year-old man

🧍

Presentation

  • Fatigue, pallor, glossitis, mild shortness of breath
  • Poor diet
  • Recent alcohol withdrawal
🧪

Laboratory

  • Hemoglobin 8.2 g/dL
  • Mean corpuscular volume 110 fL — macrocytic
  • Serum folate low
  • Homocysteine elevated
  • Methylmalonic acid NORMAL
  • Smear: macrocytosis, hypersegmented neutrophils

Q: Before you read on — what is your diagnosis, and what is the single lab value that settles it?

Answer

Megaloblastic anemia due to folate deficiency. The value that settles it is the normal methylmalonic acid — elevated in B12 deficiency, normal in folate deficiency, while homocysteine rises in both. The alcohol history is the classic risk factor for folate deficiency through poor intake. Note the trap built into the case: with poor diet and alcohol you might reach for iron deficiency, but the high mean corpuscular volume rules that out — in iron deficiency it would be low.

Management: Oral folic acid supplementation and dietary improvement — considerably easier to treat than pernicious anemia. But the safety step is explicit: also send a B12 level before or alongside treatment, because folate alone would mask a coexisting B12 deficiency while its neurologic damage progressed.

Case 4 — 68-year-old woman

🧍

Presentation

  • Fatigue, mild dyspnea on exertion, pallor
  • No recent bleeding
  • Long-standing rheumatoid arthritis — chronic inflammation from autoimmune disease
🧪

Laboratory

  • Hemoglobin 9.5 g/dL
  • Mean corpuscular volume 88 fL — normocytic
  • Serum iron low
  • Ferritin normal to high
  • Total iron binding capacity low
  • Reticulocyte count low

Q: Before you read on — what is your diagnosis, and what is the single lab value that settles it?

Answer

Anemia of chronic disease, driven by chronic inflammation from rheumatoid arthritis. The discriminating pair is ferritin normal-to-high with a LOW total iron binding capacity. Serum iron is low in both this and iron deficiency, so it decides nothing — but in true iron deficiency the ferritin would be low and the TIBC high. Here they point the opposite way, which means the iron exists and is being withheld rather than being absent. The low reticulocyte count confirms a production problem, and the normocytic index is typical.

Management: Manage the underlying rheumatoid arthritis — controlling the inflammation corrects the anemia. Consider erythropoiesis-stimulating agents if she is symptomatic, weighing the real safety concerns against severity. And optimize her diet: note that a 68-year-old living alone may well have concurrent nutritional deficiencies.

Glossary and Abbreviations

Every abbreviation and technical term used in this file, expanded and defined. If a term appears anywhere above without its long form, it is here.

Cells and structures
Erythrocyte
A red blood cell. A biconcave, anucleate disc that carries oxygen on hemoglobin. Lifespan about 120 days.
Reticulocyte
A newly released, immature red cell still containing residual RNA — the lecture's “baby red cell.” The count tells you whether the marrow is responding.
Megakaryocyte
A very large marrow cell that fragments its own membrane to produce platelets. It becomes large by endomitosis — nuclear division without cell division.
Platelet
An anucleate membrane fragment from a megakaryocyte; the first cell to arrive at a vascular injury.
Neutrophil
The most abundant granulocyte; first responder to bacterial infection. Normally has three to five nuclear lobes.
Eosinophil / basophil
Granulocytes involved chiefly in allergy and parasitic defense.
Monocyte
A circulating phagocyte that becomes a tissue macrophage or dendritic cell.
Plasma cell
A terminally differentiated B lymphocyte that secretes antibody — the humoral immune response.
Trabeculae
The internal bony struts inside a bone, visible as bright pink bands on a marrow biopsy.
Stroma
The supporting, non-hematopoietic cells of the marrow — fibroblasts, osteoblasts, adipocytes, endothelium.
Measurements
CBC — complete blood count
The standard automated panel: hemoglobin, hematocrit, red cell indices, white cell count with differential, and platelet count.
H&H
Shorthand for hemoglobin and hematocrit.
Hgb — hemoglobin
The oxygen-carrying protein, measured directly by spectrophotometry, in grams per deciliter (g/dL). Four subunits — two alpha, two beta — each carrying one oxygen molecule.
Hct — hematocrit
The percentage of whole blood volume that is red cells, measured by centrifugation. Also called packed cell volume.
MCV — mean corpuscular volume
Average red cell size in femtoliters (fL). Under 80 microcytic, 80–100 normocytic, over 100 macrocytic.
MCH — mean corpuscular hemoglobin
Average hemoglobin mass per red cell, in picograms. Underlies the terms hypochromic and normochromic.
MCHC
Mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration — hemoglobin per unit red cell volume. Characteristically high in hereditary spherocytosis.
RDW
Red cell distribution width — the variability in cell size. Raised when two populations coexist.
LDH — lactate dehydrogenase
An intracellular enzyme released when cells are destroyed; elevated in hemolysis and in ineffective erythropoiesis.
Descriptive morphology
Normocytic / microcytic / macrocytic
Normal / small / large red cells, by mean corpuscular volume.
Normochromic / hypochromic
Normal / reduced hemoglobin content per cell. Hypochromia shows as an enlarged central pale zone.
Central pallor
The pale middle of a normal red cell, created by its biconcave shape. Normally about a third of the diameter.
Macro-ovalocyte
A large, oval red cell — characteristic of megaloblastic anemia.
Hypersegmented neutrophil
A neutrophil with six or more nuclear lobes. Near-diagnostic of B12 or folate deficiency.
Megaloblast
A large, immature erythroid precursor with fine, open chromatin, seen in the marrow in B12 or folate deficiency.
Anisocytosis / poikilocytosis
Variation in red cell size / variation in red cell shape.
Cellularity
The proportion of marrow occupied by hematopoietic cells rather than fat: normocellular, hypercellular, or hypocellular.
Iron
Fe²⁺ / Fe³⁺
Ferrous / ferric iron. Only the ferrous form is absorbed from the gut.
Transferrin
The plasma protein that transports iron; picture it carrying cups that may be full or empty.
TIBC — total iron binding capacity
A measure of the transferrin binding sites not saturated with iron. Rises in iron deficiency, falls in inflammation.
Transferrin saturation
The percentage of transferrin binding sites occupied by iron. Under 15% suggests iron deficiency.
Ferritin
The intracellular iron storage protein; the serum level reflects total body stores. Also an acute phase reactant, so it rises in inflammation regardless of stores.
Hemosiderin
An insoluble aggregated form of stored iron, found chiefly in macrophages.
Hepcidin
The liver hormone, driven up by interleukin-6, that degrades ferroportin and blocks iron export from cells.
Ferroportin
The only cellular iron export channel — the door hepcidin locks.
Prussian blue stain
A histochemical stain for iron. Blue granules present means stores exist; absence is diagnostic of iron deficiency.
Pica
Craving and consumption of non-nutritive substances. Craving ice specifically is pagophagia, strongly associated with iron deficiency.
FOBT — fecal occult blood test
Detects blood in stool that is not visible; used to pursue an occult gastrointestinal source of iron loss.
Vitamin B12 and folate
Cobalamin
Vitamin B12. Obtained from animal products; plants contain very little.
IF — intrinsic factor
A protein secreted by gastric parietal cells; B12 must bind it to be absorbed in the terminal ileum.
Haptocorrin
A salivary binding protein that carries B12 through the stomach before it is handed to intrinsic factor.
Transcobalamin II
The plasma protein that carries absorbed B12 to the tissues.
Parietal cell
A gastric mucosal cell that secretes both hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor.
MMA — methylmalonic acid
A metabolite that accumulates in B12 deficiency and stays normal in folate deficiency. The key discriminator.
Homocysteine
Elevated in both B12 and folate deficiency, so it cannot separate them.
THF — tetrahydrofolate
The active form of folate, required for thymidine and therefore DNA synthesis.
Pernicious anemia
Autoimmune destruction of gastric mucosa causing loss of parietal cells and intrinsic factor, and therefore B12 deficiency.
Subacute combined degeneration
Degeneration of the dorsal and lateral columns of the spinal cord from B12 deficiency. Eventually irreversible.
Schilling test
A historical staged urinary test that localized the cause of B12 malabsorption to intrinsic factor or the terminal ileum.
Glossitis
A smooth, sore, inflamed tongue; seen in B12, folate, and iron deficiency.
Mechanisms and general terms
Hematopoiesis
Blood cell production and development from hematopoietic stem cells.
Erythropoiesis / thrombopoiesis / myelopoiesis / lymphopoiesis
Production of red cells / platelets / granulocytes and monocytes / lymphocytes.
EPO — erythropoietin
The kidney hormone that stimulates red cell production. Available as a drug (epoetin, darbepoetin).
TPO — thrombopoietin
The hormone that drives platelet production.
G-CSF / GM-CSF
Granulocyte, and granulocyte-macrophage, colony-stimulating factor. Drive white cell production; given as filgrastim and sargramostim.
Ineffective erythropoiesis
Precursors are produced but destroyed within the marrow before release — hypercellular marrow with a low reticulocyte count.
Acute phase reactant
A protein whose level changes with inflammation independent of its usual function. Ferritin rises; transferrin falls.
Hemophagocytosis
Macrophages consuming blood cells. Augmented in severe inflammation.
AOCD — anemia of chronic disease
Also called anemia of inflammation. Impaired production plus iron sequestration driven by cytokines.
Aplastic
Absence of production. An aplastic crisis is a sudden shutdown of red cell production, classically from parvovirus B19.
MDS — myelodysplastic syndrome
A clonal marrow disorder with ineffective, dysplastic hematopoiesis.
Polycythemia
An elevated hematocrit — the opposite of anemia.
Extramedullary hematopoiesis
Blood production outside the marrow, in liver and spleen, when demand is extreme.

🎯 Hematopoiesis & Anemia I — High-Yield One-Pager

UNE COM · condensed by learning objective — normal hematopoiesis · defining and classifying anemia · the four production failures

Normal hematopoiesis · LO 1–6

Definition & sites

  • Hematopoiesis = blood cell production from hematopoietic stem cells; begins in embryonic life, continues in specialized microenvironments.
  • Sites over time: yolk sac → fetal liver & spleen → bone marrow.
  • Adult: marrow of vertebrae, ribs, sternum, pelvis (axial skeleton).
  • Spun blood = plasma / buffy coat (WBC+platelets) / erythrocytes. Plasma should be yellow; pink = intravascular hemolysis.

Stem cell hierarchy

  • HSC properties: self-renewal + differentiation; multipotent.
  • Myeloid: erythrocytes, megakaryocytes→platelets, neutrophils, eos, basos, monocytes→macrophage/dendritic.
  • Lymphoid: T (thymus), B (marrow)→plasma cell, NK.
  • Platelets = anucleate membrane fragments blebbed from megakaryocytes.
  • HSCs over-self-renewing = leukemia.

Hormonal regulation

  • Erythropoietin — kidney → red cells. Lab: Hct/Hgb/retic.
  • Thrombopoietin → platelets. Lab: platelet count.
  • G-CSF / GM-CSF → granulocytes & monocytes. Lab: WBC differential.
  • Growth hormone, IGF → lymphocytes.
  • Retic low = production problem. Retic high = loss/destruction.

Niche & biopsy

  • Niche = stromal cells, extracellular matrix, vessels, signaling molecules; balances quiescence vs activation.
  • Biopsy: prone, posterior superior iliac spine, sedation, trocar. Aspirate = cytology; core = architecture/cellularity.
  • Hypercellular → leukemia or compensatory drive. Hypocellular → aplastic anemia, MDS, post-chemo/transplant.
  • Do NOT biopsy for routine anemia workup.
Defining & classifying anemia · LO 1–2

Definitions & measurement

  • Physiologic: reduced oxygen-carrying capacity. Laboratory: reduced circulating red cell mass by Hgb or Hct.
  • Hgb = spectrophotometry, g/dL. Hct = spun percentage of red cells. Hct ≈ 3 × Hgb.
  • Normal Hct: female 37–47%, male 42–52%. Elevated = polycythemia.
  • Symptoms: pallor, weakness, dyspnea on exertion; severe → myocardial and CNS hypoxia.

Indices

  • MCV <80 microcytic · 80–100 normocytic · >100 macrocytic.
  • MCH → normochromic / hypochromic (enlarged central pallor) / hyperchromic.
  • Normal RBC = biconcave disc, central pallor ≈ ⅓ diameter, highly deformable.
  • A normal MCV can hide combined micro + macrocytic disease — check RDW and the smear.

Three mechanism buckets

  • Blood loss — acute (trauma) / chronic (GI, gynecologic).
  • Impaired production — iron, B12/folate, anemia of chronic disease.
  • Increased destruction — intrinsic (membrane/spherocytosis, enzyme/G6PD, thalassemia, sickle) or extrinsic (antibody, mechanical, hypersplenism).
  • Acute hemorrhage: initial Hgb can be normal — concentration unchanged.

MCV differential

  • Micro: iron deficiency; thalassemia; AOCD (low-normal); sideroblastic; lead.
  • Normo: AOCD; acute blood loss; chronic kidney disease; hemolysis; marrow failure.
  • Macro: B12; folate; alcohol; liver; hypothyroid; MDS; drugs; reticulocytosis.
The four production failures · LO 3–5

Iron deficiency

  • Most common nutritional deficiency worldwide. 80% body iron in Hgb/myoglobin/enzymes, 20% stored.
  • Stations: duodenum → transferrin → cells → ferritin.
  • Causes: dietary lack (infants/elderly/milk-only); malabsorption (sprue, gastrectomy); ↑ requirement (pregnancy, growth); chronic blood loss (most important).
  • Adult male or postmenopausal female = GI blood loss until proven otherwise → colonoscopy.
  • Labs: Fe ↓, ferritin ↓, TIBC ↑, saturation ↓ (<15%), MCV ↓, marrow iron absent.
  • Ferritin is an acute phase reactant — can be falsely normal/high.

B12 & pernicious anemia

  • B12 does DNA synthesis + myelin. Source: animal products.
  • Path: pepsin → haptocorrin → pancreatic proteases → intrinsic factor (parietal cells) → terminal ileum → transcobalamin II.
  • Megaloblastic: macro-ovalocytes, hypersegmented neutrophils (≥6 lobes), hypercellular marrow, low retic, high LDH = ineffective erythropoiesis.
  • Pernicious anemia = autoimmune loss of parietal cells → no IF. Anti-parietal cell 85–90%, anti-IF 75%.
  • PA tissue triad: megaloblastic anemia + gastric atrophy (→ gastric carcinoma risk) + subacute combined degeneration (dorsal & lateral columns).
  • Labs: MCV ↑, MMA elevated, homocysteine elevated, B12 low.

Folate

  • Identical megaloblastic anemia, NO neurologic manifestations.
  • Key for neural tube closure — prevents spina bifida.
  • Causes: alcoholism, poor intake; pregnancy/infancy; folate antagonists (methotrexate).
  • Labs: MCV ↑, serum & RBC folate low, homocysteine ↑, MMA NORMAL.
  • Never give folate alone — corrects B12 anemia while neurologic damage progresses.

Anemia of chronic disease

  • Most common anemia in hospitalized US patients. Defective iron utilization — mimics iron deficiency.
  • Causes: chronic infection (osteomyelitis, abscess, endocarditis); immune (RA, Crohn); neoplasm.
  • Mechanism: cytokines → ↑ hepcidin (locks ferroportin), ↓ erythropoietin, ↓ erythroid proliferation, ↑ hemophagocytosis.
  • Labs: MCV low-normal, Fe ↓, TIBC ↓, ferritin ↑, marrow iron increased in macrophages.
  • Treat the underlying disease. Oral iron does not work.
